 Photo: Apple TV 
 Throughout six seasons of Slow Horses , Diana Taverner has served as a worthy foil to Jackson Lamb because she projects an air of buttoned-down hypercompetence and enough deviance to succeed at whatever game of four-dimensional chess she’s playing at one time or another. And she’s looked even better when placed alongside obvious boobs like Peter Judd or Claude Whelan, the latter of whom spent the fourth and fifth season stepping on rakes as First Desk while she waited in the wings. Now that she’s made her ascent to Whelan’s job, which she’d coveted for so long, the crown would feel heavy, but there’s no reason to suspect it’ll strain her neck too much. She has to be a step ahead of the action, right? Right?! 
 And yet, Taverner spends much of this week’s action-packed episode getting dressed down and compromised by the type of men she’s used to outmaneuvering, and she’s running out of time to regain the upper hand. At a particularly low moment, when she’s called before a committee led by the Home secretary, Taverner tries to manage the fallout from her interview on Cantor’s network by painting her predecessors as more inept, which isn’t the most stirring defense of her brief tenure so far as First Desk. Claude Whelan is an awfully low bar to clear.
 The deeper blunder is her handling of the off-the-books assassination of a Russian agent in Kazan, ordered in response to nerve attacks on British soil, and at least there she can legitimately spread the blame around. She cannot do her job with the paltry budget she’s allotted by the government, and she cannot pull off a dramatic action like Kazan if she’s gummed up by bureaucracy. As she tells the committee, “I’m expected to manage the safety of this country with the funds of a village fête. It’s like being sent into a gunfight with a pencil. A pencil that requires a subcommittee’s approval.”
 The committee isn’t fully aware of the muddy bog in which Taverner is currently sinking, but Lamb is starting to understand the shape of it. Arriving unannounced in her office, he notices the luxury gift basket Cantor has messaged her for doing the interview and isn’t beneath teasing her for selling out. When she tries to explain that Cantor was merely “investing” in national security, he scoffs at the insult to his intelligence, saying, “If you took his money, he owns every last inch of you.” But whatever Schadenfreude Lamb might be feeling about his rival’s humiliation is checked by concern over how much her operation has compromised his agents, past and present. It’s always part of the Slow Horses formula for Lamb to feel protective of his sad little flock, and there’s never been a time when they’ve been this exposed.
 To that end, the bulk of the episode is about that exposure, with Lamb’s joes still scrambling for safety on multiple fronts. As with the previous hour, which opened with the Russian assassins stalking River and Sid at the bowling alley, this episode picks up at the suspense cliffhanger of these same assassins peeling off with an abducted Sid in their car. This leads to River commandeering a woman’s car and inadvertently gaining a partner in her dog Monty, who doesn’t figure into the action but is most assuredly a Very Good Boy. The question of why the assassins kidnap Sid rather than kill her outright doesn’t get much of an answer, since they talk openly in the car about hanging her from a tree or setting her on fire. She’s granted James Bond status in that the villains cannot simply shoot her like they have everyone else. They have to make her death more elaborate and escapable.
 And escape Sid does, through the novelty license plate she slips out of her coat sleeve and jams into the neck of the Russian woman driving the car, which subsequently flips over and allows her to crawl to freedom, bloodied but unbowed. As the male assassin finds her and nearly drowns her in a lake, River catches up to the scene in time to save her, and the episode shifts to accommodate the romantic chemistry that’s been simmering between them since the series premiere. They talk quietly about his grandfather’s funeral, and the conversation continues when the Dogs locate them and shuttle them unexpectedly to an airport hangar, where a plane awaits to take Sid to an unknown destination.
 At this point, Sid finally gets the conversation with Taverner that she’s been risking her life to have — and, ironically, she understands it as her death notice. Taverner is frank about her plans to turn Sid over to the GRU because she needs to de-escalate tensions and she cannot afford to lose the agent who carried out the hit in Kazan. But her subsequent promise to bring Sid back in two months doesn’t pass the smell test, and when Taverner’s assistant on the other end of the call later notes that the flight is going through Bulgaria, not Moscow, it’s a sign that the Russians will be free to do what they want. Sid is smart enough to sniff this out, and the show seizes the opportunity to raise the romantic stakes through an adorably British expression of mutual libidinousness. Sid saying, “I’d leave the light on at your grandfather’s house” is enough of a sexual enticement for River to risk his neck to keep the Dogs from putting her on that plane.
 With so much drama surrounding Taverner and Sid, in particular, the episode keeps most of the other characters on the back burner until next week’s finale. While Lamb continues to look into Cantor’s connection to the Russians, which leads to him briefly tracking Cantor’s contact Natasha, the safe house where Catherine, Louisa, Shirley, and Moira are hiding out gets more crowded, as Flyte, Roddy, and Reece pile into the place. The fact that it’s Taverner’s vacation home has become a solid running joke as they make a deeper mess of the place, with Shirley improvising Molotov cocktails out of Taverner’s extensive liquor collection. Not long ago, Flyte was right-hand to First Desk, and now she’s stuck with the dregs of Slough House, babysitting Roddy and Reece while they all wait like sitting ducks for Harkness to turn up. If Sid weren’t on the blocks as a doomed trading piece, then Flyte would have a case as the person most egregiously wronged by Taverner’s mistakes.
 With Harkness and the female Russian assassin still in the wind — and Sid most definitely not on a plane to Bulgaria — next week’s finale is shaping up to add more bodies to a death-haunted season.
 Shots 
 • A perfectly British reaction to having your ride commandeered: “It’s not very convenient. I need it. I need the car.”
 • The Russian assassins have been doing their deadly job with cool efficiency, so it’s notable that they’re so openly sadistic about how they want to kill Sid. They sincerely believe that she killed one of their own and that getting revenge is personal to them.
 • Funny line from River about how getting stalked by assassins has kept him from dwelling on his grandfather’s death: “Maybe that’s how it works with traumas. One cancels out the other.”
 • Cantor is such an absolute boob that it’s hard to believe Natasha’s promise of “the biggest distribution deal in Russian history” will ever come to pass. He is definitely a useful idiot.
 • Slow Horses fans should be aware that Rosalind Eleazar, the actress who plays Louisa, has the title role in Misty Green , Chris Rock’s first film as director since 2014’s Top Five . Vulture critic Alison Willmore has mixed-to-negative feelings about the film, but she’s not alone in considering Eleazar “outstanding” in the lead.
